sources.text:
Caitlin Clark Calls Out the Media—And Gets Backup From Obama
Caitlin Clark is rightfully pushing back against attacks on her character and the way she has been covered in the media.
"I think there's a false characterization of who I am sometimes," Clark said in an interview with ESPN's Malika Andrews from WNBA All-Star weekend in Chicago.
"I get people have a job to do, but at the same time, don't make accusations about my character and who I am when you don't know me," she added.
The Indiana Fever star specifically called out the media for how things around her have been framed.
"I feel like media and journalism have a responsibility to tell the stories. A lot of times you guys are the ones controlling the narratives about what people read and what people talk about it. A lot of that is sometimes so far out of touch with what is reality. And that can be confusing to somebody that's 24 and trying to navigate life and trying to help her team win a championship," Clark said.
The infamous flagrant foul she was on the receiving end of from Phoenix Mercury star Alyssa Thomas was then brought up, with Clark clearly conveying that the subsequent discourse can weigh on her.
"It seems like there's always a moment like that in every season that I've so far," she said in sharing how that should have been handled properly in the moment and quickly moved on from.
"When I walk out of the locker room I shouldn't be, not fearful of what the conversation is gonna be, but it's emotionally exhausting, it's draining, it makes your shoulders tense because people don't want to talk about the basketball, they just want to stir it up and make it something else."
Case in point: A recent unhinged column from Nancy Armour of USA Today became a subject of conversation. It's shameful that the piece even made it to print, as among other slights at Clark and characterizations of her fans, Armour somehow drew a parallel between Clark pleading for a better whistle from referees and the lynching of 14-year-old Emmett Till in 1955.
The idea that anyone could think that, much less print it in a major publication, was only further proof of just how far off the rails the conversation around Clark has gone.
Barack Obama Embrace Hopefully Signals Shift
Clark's plight has not gone unnoticed by former President Barack Obama.
Obama made an appearance at WNBA All-Star media day and made it a point to offer Clark some words of support and encouragement.
"You're great. You're fantastic. Don't let all this nonsense get you down," Obama said after approaching Clark.
He then relayed how he didn't get famous until he was older in showing an appreciation for everything she has had to manage at such a young age.
"Don't lose that joy. The game is like the game. And you're hooper."
The words from Obama were kind, wise, and correct. Clark is certainly hooping, as are the Fever as a whole.
She recently set a career-high with 45 points in a win over the Seattle Storm, which was also the first-ever 40-point 10-assist game in WNBA history. Overall, she is fourth in the league in scoring and second in assists, despite having to play under a minutes restriction after a return from injury. Indiana has won five of six games and are on pace to set a new record for points per game.
There is absolutely no reason all of that should be overshadowed by media coverage that elevates the worst aspects of social media or takes unjustified shots at Clark as a person and what she stands for.
It's nice to see her push back on what Obama appropriately described as "nonsense," just like it was heartwarming to see him seek her out to provide encouragement.
Hopefully it serves as a way to shift things back where they belong: basketball. Because there are plenty of great stories to cover there when it comes to Clark and her Fever teammates.

sources.news_title: Obama drops in on WNBA All-Stars at his Presidential Center — and the league rolls out the red carpet
sources.text:
Former President Barack Obama made a surprise visit to WNBA All-Stars practicing at his recently opened Presidential Center, drawing gushing praise from players and league officials eager to celebrate the moment.
Obama walked onto the basketball court before practice on Friday and addressed the assembled players, spending several minutes speaking to the group before posing for a group photo and then roughly ten minutes shaking hands and snapping individual pictures with the stars. He received a No. 44 WNBA All-Star jersey, a nod to his place as the 44th president, and even dropped into a defensive stance for a brief, playful exchange with New York Liberty star Jonquel Jones, CBS News Chicago reported.
The visit took place at the Obama Presidential Center, which opened last month. WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert noted that the league was the first professional sports organization to use the facility’s basketball court, a distinction she tied to the WNBA’s 30th anniversary celebration.
Engelbert did not miss the chance to lavish praise on the former president:
“It’s fitting for our 30th anniversary that we’re here as the first sports league to play in the Obama Presidential Center. Someone who has inspired hundreds of millions of people to dream big and accomplish things like President Obama has and his tie to basketball is amazing, too. I think there’s no more fitting person to be meeting with the players.”
For a league that has struggled for decades to build a stable audience, the WNBA’s eagerness to bask in Obama’s reflected glow is understandable. Whether it translates into lasting viewership or revenue is another question entirely.
Caitlin Clark calls the meeting a lifelong memory
Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark, arguably the single biggest driver of the WNBA’s recent surge in attention, spoke to reporters after the visit. She called the encounter “obviously super cool” and said Obama had complimented her on how she handles public scrutiny.
Clark relayed Obama’s personal advice:
“He’s somebody that has been in front of the media quite a bit and he reminded me, ‘When I got famous in my 40s, I didn’t have to do it in my 20s.'”
Clark described it as “a moment I’ll probably remember for the rest of my life.” AP News confirmed the exchange, noting Obama spent personal time with Clark and acknowledged the pressures she faces in the public eye.
Obama’s broader remarks to the group leaned into the league’s growth narrative. He told players the game “has been picking up and people paying attention to your excellence,” adding that watching it “has been making me happy.” He also thanked them for off-court work inspiring young people.
The Obama Presidential Center itself drew criticism when it opened, with detractors calling it more of an activism headquarters than a traditional presidential library. Friday’s event, blending sports, celebrity, and civic programming, fit that mold. After meeting the players, Obama spoke to a group of investors and nearly 100 high school girls at the center.
Jones bumped Obama on the court, and he bumped back
The lightest moment of the visit came courtesy of Jonquel Jones, who decided to test the former president’s basketball instincts after the photo session wound down. Jones grabbed a ball and approached Obama on the court.
“I feel like as a hooper, you know when someone’s challenging you. So I was just like, let me go over there with the basketball, you know, do a little cross, bump him a little bit. And I knew that I would get him activated a little because he’s a hooper, too.”
Obama obliged, dropping into a defensive stance for a few seconds before the moment passed. He told the group he no longer plays five-on-five to protect his Achilles tendon, but said he had broken in the center’s court with a game of “horse.”
Jones, who said she had met Obama once before, called him “a role model” and praised his family’s continued community involvement. Obama has a long history with women’s basketball. He became the first sitting U.S. president to attend a WNBA game in 2010, sitting courtside with his daughter Sasha at a Washington Mystics game. He also hosted WNBA championship and NCAA title-winning players at the White House during his presidency.
Obama’s political record, of course, extends well beyond basketball courts. His administration’s immigration policies continue to generate headlines, including cases where illegal immigrants released under his watch later faced serious criminal charges.
All-Star weekend brings Chicago connections front and center
The All-Star Game, scheduled for Saturday, carries a strong Chicago flavor. The Chicago Sky are one of four teams with a player in the game, and five former Sky players will participate. Angel Reese, formerly of the Sky, is making her third straight All-Star appearance and playing on a team managed by Cynthia Cooper.
The opposing squad is managed by Teresa Weatherspoon, the former Sky head coach. Reese has maintained a close relationship with Weatherspoon since playing for her as a rookie in Chicago two years ago.
Former WNBA Finals MVP Kaleah Copper, another former Sky player, will also suit up Saturday. Obama said he would not attend the game itself, citing a prior engagement with his wife Michelle.
Obama’s post-presidential public life has kept him in the spotlight on multiple fronts. He recently warned about Justice Department politicization in a television appearance, a caution that struck many observers as inconsistent with his own administration’s record. His broader orbit of former aides has also produced its share of unflattering stories, including a former press aide fired from a six-figure city job under embarrassing circumstances.
None of that dimmed the WNBA’s enthusiasm on Friday. The league got its photo op, the players got their presidential audience, and Obama got to remind everyone he is still the most polished political brand in the Democratic Party, even on a basketball court.
The WNBA can celebrate its 30th anniversary however it likes. But borrowed star power is no substitute for a business model that stands on its own.

Obama, who’s no stranger to the sport, showed up to watch and meet the players himself. He gave a short speech, then went around greeting everyone individually. His advice prompted Caitlin Clark to humbly reply, “I try, sometimes.”
But Obama quickly disagreed and further added, “No, you’re always hooping! And you’re on a nice little run right now.”

He’s somebody that has been in front of the media quite a bit… And sometimes I think people don’t always realize I’m 24 years old, and I’m trying to navigate a lot of different things while trying to play basketball at the same time.”

Definitely a moment I’ll probably remember for the rest of my life. My hands don’t usually get pretty sweaty and clammy for certain things, but it did for that,” she added.
With the WNBA All-Star Game set for Saturday night at the United Center, Caitlin Clark will once again be in the spotlight. But after Obama’s words of encouragement, she’ll head into the showcase with a simple reminder: tune out the noise, keep hooping, and don’t lose the joy of the game.

It’s WNBA All-Star weekend in Chicago, and Angel Reese is already making headlines. In addition to launching her new Signature Mattel Barbie doll, the former Chicago Sky player got a few chuckles out of the media when she said her private jet was delayed because of former President Barack Obama‘s sudden arrival. Also during All-Star weekend, Reese boasted about the selfie she was able to take with the former leader of the free world, saying she had to seize the moment when it presented itself.
Angel Reese Says Her Private Jet Was Delayed In Chicago Due To President Barack Obama

All-Star weekend is here, and to kick off the slew of events, WNBA stars spoke with the media about the league’s first-ever collaboration with the Barack Obama Presidential Center in Chicago.
Reese, an Atlanta Dream player, is one of the 22 All-Stars set to take the court this weekend, but before she could even deboard her plane in the Windy City, she said she was delayed due to a certain VIP’s arrival.
“When my plane was landing yesterday … they said, ‘VIP. Nobody can get off the plane,'” Reese said. As she continued, the LSU alum said that she was confused because she, too, is a very important person. “And then they said, ‘Obama.’ And I was like, ‘OK, OK, OK,'” she joked.

— WNBA (@WNBA) July 24, 2026
President Obama had the All-Stars hyped before they became the first to hit the court at the Obama Presidential Center! pic.twitter.com/Jp4s0LkKc6
A handful of WNBA stars are living it up this weekend at the newly opened Obama Presidential Center in Chicago’s historic Jackson Park neighborhood. Among the stars are Paige Bueckers, Courtney Williams, Aja Wilson, Kahleeah Copper, and, of course, Reese.
Reese even snapped a quick selfie with the former POTUS, sharing it on her X account and writing, “Hi Mr. @BarackObama.”
Reese shared with the media why it was important for her to capture the special moment with Barack, saying, “Not everybody just gets to meet Barack.”
She continued, “That was my first time too. Baby, you got to get your (selfie). I’m getting a picture of everybody. I got one of (Copper), got one of me, a selfie. I think it’s important just to capture every moment.”
The WNBA Is The First Professional League To Team Up With The Obama Presidential Center
According to a previous report from The Blast, the WNBA is the very first professional league to join forces with the Obama Presidential Center. In addition to today’s media event at the historic museum, the Presidential Center will also host the third annual WNBA Changemaker Day and the Jr. WNBA Day, which is designed to inspire young girls through sport and learning.
“Hosting AT&T WNBA All-Star events at the Obama Presidential Center is a true honor and reflects our commitment to creating connection through basketball and engaging communities in meaningful ways,” WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert said. “We’re excited to bring together the WNBA family and the greater Chicago community to create memorable experiences at this historic new venue.”
Angel Reese Is A Barbie!
To celebrate Reese’s third consecutive All-Star weekend, the 24-year-old teamed up with Barbie to launch her own Signature doll.
She becomes the second WNBA player with her own doll and the first Black WNBA player to receive the honor.
The doll resembles Reese to a T and comes with all-pink attire, a matching leg sleeve, and custom “Barbie” Angel Reese 1 Reebok sneakers.
“Having my own Barbie doll is a true dream come true for me. It’s such an incredible honor because it’s about showing girls that there are no limits to what they can achieve,” said Reese, according to The Blast. “I’ve never let anyone else define what’s possible for me, and every challenge I’ve faced has only made me stronger. I hope this doll reminds girls to be unapologetically themselves, embrace every part of who they are, and go after their dreams with confidence.”
A New AR1 Sneaker Is Coming, Too
And the AR1 basketball shoe isn’t just for the doll. Reebok is actually launching a new “Barbie” colorway on August 3, featuring shades of pink, blue, and yellow.
“We’re proud to see her Barbie doll debut wearing Angel Reese 1 basketball shoes in this vibrant new Barbie colorway and to bring that same style directly to fans,” said CEO of Reebok Todd Krinsky. “This moment celebrates Angel’s impact on sport, style, and culture while giving fans the chance to match Angel’s iconic look and be part of the moment.”

sources.text:
Fourteen-year-old London Harris has dreams of someday being president of the United States, and on Friday morning she got to see a former commander in chief up close.
Former President Barack Obama surprised London, along with nearly 100 other ninth grade girls, during the third annual WNBA Changemaker Day at the recently opened Obama Presidential Center.
“It felt very surreal,” said London, a student at Dyett High School in Washington Park. “I was genuinely happy to see him and to listen to what he had to say.”
Obama popped into the center’s Elie Wiesel Auditorium just as a panel of speakers was discussing the power of perseverance.
“I know you’re all learning the power of perseverance, the power of resilience, the power of dreaming big,” WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert told the crowd. “And this person ... has inspired hundreds of millions of people around the world and here in the United States.”
Obama then walked on stage to thunderous applause.
“Hello, everybody!” Obama exclaimed, wearing jeans and a white button-down shirt.
“Settle down now,” he said, smiling, as the crowd screamed.
“I wasn’t gonna let a bunch of amazing young athletes, scholars, hoopers come through my spot without saying hello,” he said. “I’m not gonna start shaking hands yet because mayhem will break loose.”
He began by telling the girls how proud he was of them and then spoke of his own experiences of being a dad to two daughters.
“Malia is now 28, Sasha is 25, but I remember like it was yesterday when they were your age,” Obama said. “We live in a world that is a lot more complicated for you guys than it was in some ways when I was coming up. There’s so much pressure and noise, and sometimes I think — especially for girls and young women — there’s social attitudes that tell you that you need to be one kind of way.”
He then encouraged the girls that they were on the right track.
“You are going to do wonderful things, and you need to have the confidence and power that’s inside you and your capacity to, you know, live out your dreams. ... You’re gonna have to work hard, and it’s not going to be easy, but I’m confident it’s gonna happen.”
Obama joked with the girls about boys being “knuckleheads” and urged them to seek guidance from others.
“One of the most important things you can do as a young person is find people who are willing to help you,” Obama said.
“Find mentors. Find people who are doing the kinds of things you want to do and learn from them,” he added. “We only see the little fishbowl that we live in, but you know, it turns out there’s a whole big world out there full of possibilities. ... The more you see out there that’s possible, the better off you’re going to be.”
Obama then joked about talking too long because he spots one of the girls “about to fall asleep.”
“I’m used to it. That’s what it’s like at the Obama dinner table,” he said.
Obama shook hands with some of the girls as they screamed, then took a selfie with the crowd before leaving the stage.
Aliyah Myles, a student at Chicago Vocational Career Academy, grew up with Obama being a constant presence in her household. She described the former president as a huge influential figure for her mother.
Next time Aliyah talks to her mother, she’ll get to tell her she shook Obama’s hand.
“I was freaking out, I was turnt, I almost passed out,” Aliyah, 14, said. “I was everywhere.”
The event kicked off just before 10 a.m. with comments from WNBA brand strategist Nina Kossoff. Friday’s gathering was among many events in Chicago this week tied to the WNBA All-Star Game, which will be held Saturday at the United Center.
“We’re powerful on our own, but when we come together, we can really make change,” Kossoff told the girls.
They also heard from a panel featuring Ari Chambers, an ESPN Journalist and commentator; Kizmet Mills, chief diversity officer at Nike; Linnae Harper, a former Chicago Sky player and now manager of athletics and sports leadership for the Obama Foundation; and Colie Edison, the WNBA’s chief growth officer.
It was the third WNBA Changemaker Day, and this year’s theme was “Finding My Superpower” — something each panelist touched on.
“When I think about the word ‘superpower,’ the first thing that comes to mind is doing the impossible,” Harper said. “My personal superpower is connecting people with their resources, providing a pathway for them to reach their goals.”
Others on the panel spoke on helping others through basketball, leadership and community efforts. The panelists then dived into explaining how they bounced back from their setbacks.

sources.text:
Former President Barack Obama surprised the players and coaches of the WNBA All-Star team Friday morning during a practice at the Obama Presidential Center.
The team — which includes A’ja Wilson and Caitlin Clark — was scheduled to practice at the Home Court on the campus of the Obama Center ahead of Saturday’s All-Star Game at the United Center. Before practice began, Obama stepped onto the court to greet players and congratulate the league on its continued growth.
“All of you are extraordinary, and I could not be a bigger fan,” Obama said. “The way that the game has been going lately, the way it’s been picking up … I think it’s been something for basketball fans generally be excited to see. It’s been making me happy.”
The All-Star practice marked the first time that the Obama Center courts have been used for a full-scale basketball event. Obama also dropped in to speak at other WNBA All-Star events Friday on the campus, including a Changemaker Day session focused on community impact.
Wilson mentioned she collaborated on an ad with one of Obama’s daughters, while former Chicago Sky forward and current Atlanta Dream All-Star Angel Reese said her foundation also is working with the Obama Foundation.
“We really were just talking hoops. You can tell he’s always been a hooper. It doesn’t leave his blood,” WNBPA President Nneka Ogwumike said. “We’ve known from the beginning that he’s followed us and is such a fan of women’s basketball. To be able to celebrate 30 years here in the Obama Center, it feels very right.”
Obama said he christened the court a month before the official opening of the presidential campus with a game of H-O-R-S-E — and admitted he lost that inaugural game.
He teased the assembled WNBA players for their relaxed approach to Friday’s practice, bowing out of going one-on-one with any of the league’s stars after briefly guarding New York Liberty center Jonquel Jones.
“I don’t run full court no more to protect my Achilles,” the former president said jokingly.
After posing for a photo opportunity, Obama took time to speak with each All-Star individually.
“Oh, my God, that was so cool,” said Kahleah Copper, the former Sky star currently with the Phoenix Mercury. “The coolest thing for me is just how personable he is. It’s so genuine. He was just like, ‘You’re having a great season. I’m super proud of you.’ I’m like, ‘OK, are you watching me?’”
Reese made sure her fellow players got photos with him, and she got a selfie, which she later posted on social media.
“Not everybody just gets to meet Barack,” she said.
It was her first time meeting Obama, though she went on Michelle Obama’s podcast previously and said it was empowering. She also had a run-in with Obama this week at the airport.
“It’s so funny because when my plane was landing yesterday, he was right next to my plane,” Reese said. “They were like, ‘VIP, nobody can get off the plane.’ And I’m like, ‘Well, we VIP too.’ And then they said Obama, and I was like, ‘Oh, OK, OK, OK.’”
LeBron news spreads
Clark spent a couple of minutes pitching the Indiana Pacers to LeBron James during her media session, even though she said, “We all know that’s not happening.”
She offered the idea of playing with Tyrese Haliburton and Pascal Siakam. She touted playing in a smaller market, saying of the Indiana fans, “This means so much to them. Indiana is a true basketball state. It’s one of the biggest basketball states in the country, and people truly care about the game there.”
Later in her interview, she received the news: LeBron was signing a two-year contract with the Philadelphia 76ers.
“No way!” she said. “I just pitched him for the Pacers. It didn’t get to him fast enough.
“The 76ers. Wow. Selfishly I wanted the Warriors because Steph and Bron would have been absolutely insane together, but they have some serious talent on the 76ers. Arguably, maybe one of the favorites in the East now with the Knicks and obviously my Pacers.”
Bayou Barbie becomes real
Reese had to pause her interview session with reporters to do her own documenting.
Las Vegas Aces guard Jackie Young was looking at the new Angel Reese Barbie doll, which was released this week, and Reese stood up to snap a photo.
Reese said her doll, which is dressed in a pink uniform, shoes and headband and has a pink ball, is a dream years in the making, since she became known as Bayou Barbie while playing at LSU.
“I used to put Barbie stuff on merch and I wasn’t really supposed to,” Reese said. “I told them I really wanted to have a Barbie doll one day, and to have a Barbie, you have to be iconic. You have to do some real things. I knew it was going to take some time because there are so many great women that are Barbie dolls and have their own doll. I knew that’s what I wanted, and I spoke that into existence.”
Reese is back in Chicago making her third WNBA All-Star appearance but her first as a member of the Dream since the Sky traded her in April.
Reese said her move to Atlanta has “been a dream come true, literally.” She said she’s playing the best she has in her career and expressed appreciation for what she has gained under coach Karl Smesko.
“I would just say my confidence and my patience,” Reese said. “He literally works on me every single day. … Sometimes I’ll be like, ‘I don’t want to do it today.’ But he’s in my ear every day. ‘Let’s go, we’re doing this.’ … It just shows how much he cares about me, and he just wants to see me get better every single day.”

Former President Barack Obama surprises WNBA All-Stars at their practice at his Presidential Center
CHICAGO (AP) — Caitlin Clark was in awe after meeting former President Barack Obama after he surprised the WNBA All-Stars on Friday at his Presidential Center.
Clark called her conversation with Obama “a moment I’ll probably remember for the rest of my life.”
“It was obviously super cool. He just complimented me for the way that I handle everything, obviously with everything that’s been going on,” the Indiana Fever star said Friday after meeting Obama. “He’s somebody that has been in front of the media quite a bit and he reminded me, ‘When I got famous in my 40s, I didn’t have to do it in my 20s.’”
Obama spoke to the players for a few minutes on the basketball court at the center which opened last month.
“Some of you I’m meeting for the first time. All of you are extraordinary and I could not be bigger fans,” Obama said. “The way the game has been growing lately, the way it’s been picking up and people paying attention to your excellence, I think it’s been something for basketball fans, generally, a sight to see. It’s been making me happy.”
He spoke to the players for a few minutes before taking a group photo. Obama then spent about 10 minutes shaking hands with the players and taking photos with them, including Clark.
“I know many of you are involved in some wonderful ventures off the court, looking out for other young people and inspiring them. I just wanted to say thanks,” Obama said.
The former president gave a shout out to A’ja Wilson in his talk to the players and then went over and chatted with her as well.
After the photo-ops were done, Obama stepped on the court and talked with New York Liberty star Jonquel Jones, getting down in a defensive stance for a few seconds on her.
“I feel like as a hooper, you know when someone’s challenging you. So I was just like, let me go over there with the basketball, you know, do a little cross, bump him a little bit,” Jones said. “And I knew that I would get him activated a little because he’s a hooper, too.”
Jones said she had met Obama once before.
“He’s a role model for me and it was nice to be able to have that moment,” Jones said. “Someone that I look up to, someone that has paved the way for a lot of people to be here and see him continuing, his family continuing to give back to the community when they’ve already done so much is just so inspirational.”
That was the extent of his time on the court. He told the players that he didn’t play 5-on-5 anymore to protect his Achilles. He did say that he broke in the court with a game of “horse.”
Obama was the first sitting U.S. President to attend a WNBA game when he and his daughter, Sasha, sat courtside in 2010 for a Washington Mystics game. He also has hosted many of them at the White House after they either won WNBA championships or NCAA titles.
Obama was gifted with a No. 44 WNBA All-Star jersey that the players were going to autograph later.
This was the first professional sport to use the basketball court at the center, which opened in June. Obama went to the NBA All-Star Game in Los Angeles in February. Obama said he unfortunately wasn’t going to be able to make the All-Star Game on Saturday because of a previous engagement with his wife, Michelle.
“It’s fitting for our 30th anniversary that we’re here as the first sports league to play in the Obama Presidential Center,” WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert said. “Someone who has inspired hundreds of millions of people to dream big and accomplish things like President Obama has and his tie to basketball is amazing, too. I think there’s no more fitting person to be meeting with the players.”
After talking to the players, Obama went across the center to talk to a group of investors in the league and nearly 100 high school girls to talk.

CHICAGO — On Friday morning, former President Barack Obama surprised players by showing up at practice.

Former First Lady Michele Obama was not with him. He gave the players a short speech and also informed them he won't be able to attend the All-Star Game due to a previous engagement.

Clark called her conversation with Obama "a moment I’ll probably remember for the rest of my life."
“It was obviously super cool. He just complimented me for the way that I handle everything, obviously with everything that’s been going on," Clark told reporters Friday morning. "He’s somebody that has been in front of the media quite a bit and he reminded me, ‘When I got famous in my 40s, I didn’t have to do it in my 20s.’
"Sometimes, I think, people don’t always realize, like, I’m 24-years-old and I’m trying to navigate a lot of different things while trying to play basketball at the same time. So, it was cool to hear that from him and I think, honestly, it’s probably a good reminder for all of us to treat people with respect, treat people with grace."
Obama also briefly played one-on-one with New York Liberty center Jonquel Jones and took a selfie with Atlanta Dream forward Angel Reese.
An $850 million facility, the Obama Presidential Center opened in June on the South Side of Chicago as the public home of President Obama’s legacy. Of the many features at the complex is a 60,000-square foot athletic building with a basketball court.
“Hopefully, the court has held up. I don’t run full-court no more to protect my Achilles," Obama said. "I did inaugurate (the court) with a game of H.O.R.S.E., which I lost. I was not happy about it.”
Obama was the first sitting U.S. President to attend a WNBA game when he and his daughter, Sasha, sat courtside for a clash between the Washington Mystics and Detroit Shock in 2010. It’s been making me happy.

Caitlin Clark’s WNBA tenure has been marred by rivalries, hard fouls, tantrums, and somehow the controversy often boils down to race.
The heightened media attention has been a lot for the 24-year-old as she navigates her popularity, but now she knows she’s at least got President Obama in her corner.
The WNBA is in the midst of its All-Star break, and since the ladies were practicing at the Barack Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, it was only right that its namesake stop by and surprise this year’s 22 All-Stars.
“Some of you I’m meeting for the first time, all of you are extraordinary,” Obama said in a brief introductory speech. “The way the game has been growing lately and the way the game has been picking up, people have been paying attention to your excellence. … It has been a sight to see.”
Other tidbits he dropped included him saying he doesn’t play 5-on-5 anymore to protect his Achilles, but he did break in the court with a game of HORSE.
After addressing the crowd, he spoke individually to some players, including Clark, and gave her some words of encouragement as she continued to adjust to newfound attention.
“You’re great. You’re fantastic. Don’t let all this nonsense get you down,” Obama said. “One of the things that was luckiest for me was, I didn’t get famous until I was like 45. So, I was an old ass man. You’re my daughters’ age; they haven’t had that much immersion in nonsense, so don’t lose that joy. The game’s, like, the game. And you’re a hooper.”
The interaction ended with Clark asking for a picture before inviting her teammates Kelsey Mitchell and Aliyah Boston to join her for a group photo.
Afterward, Clark spoke about the interaction and how it was a breath of fresh air to hear someone else acknowledge what it’s like juggling all her newfound responsibilities.
“Sometimes I think people don’t always realize, like, I’m 24 years old, and I’m trying to navigate a lot of different things while trying to play basketball,” Clark said. “So, it was cool to hear that from him. And I think honestly, it’s a good reminder to treat people with respect, treat people with grace. It’s definitely a moment I’ll remember for the rest of my life.”

These kind words come after a June 24 game between the Phoenix Mercury and Indiana Fever where Alyssa Thomas appeared to shove her hand in Clark’s neck. No foul was called in real time, but Thomas was eventually suspended for a game.
It led to Republican lawmakers attempting to intervene, claiming the league was allowing WNBA players to “attack” Clark.

These kind words come after a June 24 game between the Phoenix Mercury and Indiana Fever where Alyssa Thomas appeared to shove her hand in Clark’s neck. No foul was called in real time, but Thomas was eventually suspended for a game.
It led to Republican lawmakers attempting to intervene, claiming the league was allowing WNBA players to “attack” Clark.
Even NBA commissioner Adam Silver has said that rhetoric around Clark has blown so much out of proportion that she’s become a “political ping pong.”

sources.news_title: Caitlin Clark weighs in on recent WNBA controversies as Barack Obama tells her to block out the ‘nonsense’
sources.text:
Clark and other All-Stars, in Chicago for the ASG, met the former president on Friday morning
Former President Barack Obama made a surprise appearance at the WNBA All-Star practice on Friday and took some time to compliment Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark on how she has handled the spotlight, particularly during a controversy-filled time in the WNBA.
“You are fantastic. Don’t let all this nonsense get you down,” Obama told Clark, a moment that was captured by NBC Chicago. “… Don’t lose that joy. The game is like, the game. And you are a hooper… you are always hooping. And you are on a nice little run right now.”
Not many things make Clark nervous, but she laughed while saying that her hands got “sweaty and clammy” during her conversation with the former president.
“He just complimented me for the way that I handle everything, obviously with everything that’s been going on,” Clark told reporters. “He’s somebody that has been in front of the media quite a bit, and he reminded me, ‘When I got famous in my 40s, I didn’t have to do it in my 20s.’
“Sometimes people don’t always realize I’m 24 years old, and I’m trying to navigate a lot of different things, while trying to play basketball at the same time. So it was cool to hear that from him. And I think, honestly, it was probably a good reminder for all of us, treating people with respect, treating people with grace. Definitely a moment I’ll probably remember for the rest of my life.”
Clark, who rose to prominence as a star at Iowa, is now in her third WNBA season. She’ll play in her second All-Star Game this week after missing last season’s in Indiana due to injury. Clark has had a recent stretch of impressive play, including the WNBA’s first 45-point, 10-assist double-double last week. However, Clark has also become the subject of a lot of recent WNBA drama.
Earlier this month, she spoke out against death threats made toward Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas following a no-call in an incident in which Thomas made contact with Clark’s throat. The call was eventually retroactively reviewed and Thomas was given a suspension. Thomas accepted the punishment but said she and other teammates were being harassed and threatened.
Officiating as a whole has been a heated topic in the sport, but protecting Clark is a subject that consistently blows up on social media. Clark, meanwhile, picked up her seventh technical foul of the season this week and is one tech away from an automatic suspension.
Everything she does seems to be analyzed and talked about, even by those who don’t follow the WNBA closely. However, Clark is trying to keep her feet on the ground and not let the noise bother her.
“There’s obviously a lot of people who like to comment on my character and think they know me,” Clark said on Friday. “At the end of the day, they have no idea who I am. I get it is an opinion and everybody is entitled to their own opinions. Whether I was a young girl or 24 (years old) with the spotlight on me, that’s never changed. Everybody has an opinion on everybody. I personally try to keep it moving. I’m going to treat everybody with respect and kindness and love. I think if everybody could do that, we’d be in a little bit better of a spot.”
Clark will not be participating in the 3-point contest on Friday, but she will suit up for the 2026 WNBA All-Star game on Saturday night.

sources.news_title: Obama greets WNBA All-Stars on Home Court
sources.text:
Former President Barack Obama surprised WNBA All-Stars on Friday morning at the Obama Presidential Center before what officials said was the first professional basketball practice at Home Court.
The WNBA's All-Stars are in Chicago for the league's annual showcase, which continues Friday night with a skills challenge at the Wintrust Arena, home of the Chicago Sky, and culminates Saturday with the All-Star Game between Team Spoon and Team Coop at the United Center.
WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert opened the event by welcoming the All-Stars to the league’s 30th anniversary season.
“We thought it was really fitting to be here at the Obama Presidential Center on our 30th anniversary season with our star athletes on this amazing court,” she said.
Michael Strautmanis, the Obama Foundation’s chief corporate affairs officer, told the players the campus was built with the idea that sports “is a pathway to do what you all do.” Home Court is the center’s 60,000-square-foot athletic and events space, located just across the street from Hyde Park Academy.
Tina Tchen, the foundation’s executive vice president and head of programs, said the practice marked the first time professional basketball players had used the court for a professional practice. She pointed out the court includes 3-point lines for both the NBA and WNBA, as a reflection of the center’s commitment to “be inclusive and intentional.”
Obama then walked onto the court, interrupting her speech and drawing loud cheers and applause from the players. He wore blue jeans and a crisp white button-down shirt.
“All of you are extraordinary, and I could not be a bigger fan,” Obama told the players. “The way the game has been going lately, the way it’s been picking up, and people paying attention to your excellence, I think has been something for basketball fans generally, a sight to see.”
Obama joked with the players about the relaxed pace during their practice, which ran at roughly a quarter speed with players jogging through drills and taking it easy on defense. He briefly guarded New York Liberty center Jonquel Jones, bending down to try to poke the ball away as she attempted to cross him over.
“I don’t run full court no more to protect my Achilles,” Obama said.
Last month, Obama tested out the Home Court ahead of the campus’s official opening on Juneteenth, playing a game of H.O.R.S.E. with confidants including Strautmanis and Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias, among others. Obama apparently lost the game.
Obama told players that, unfortunately, he would not attend Saturday’s All-Star Game because of a commitment involving Michelle Obama.
“I'm sorry about that, but I don't mess with my wife,” Obama said.
For several players, Friday marked their first meeting with the former president. Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark, one of two team captains for Saturday’s game, chatted with Obama upon meeting him individually before snagging a photo with him and a couple of teammates.
“You have to pinch yourself,” Clark said after meeting Obama on All-Star Weekend.
Minnesota Lynx guard Courtney Williams, who missed the first shot of the practice with an airball, described her introduction to Obama as “smooth.”
“I feel like it was love, bro,” she said. “For him to pull up and show his love, that was dope.”
Lynx rookie guard Olivia Miles, 23, an All-Star starter in her first season, said meeting Obama felt surreal given she grew up learning about his presidency from her parents.
“It’s definitely cool,” she said. “I didn’t think we would have the opportunity to do so, let alone meet him.”
Las Vegas Aces center A’ja Wilson, a three-time MVP and Team Spoon starter, had met Obama before and was less star-struck. She said her routine these days revolves around staying healthy and not much else.
“I'm a little boring,” she said. “If I’m not sleeping, I’m eating. If I’m not eating, I’m in my car heading to the gym.”
Former Sky standout Angel Reese let out a scream after greeting Obama, before returning to practice drills that included lefty and righty layups. Reese was traded to the Dream in April for two future first-round picks and is playing in her second All-Star Game Saturday.
No Sky players are on either All-Star roster this year. The Sky enter the weekend with a 9-18 record, the third-worst mark in the WNBA.
Elsewhere during the practice session, Dallas Wings guard Paige Bueckers, Toronto Tempo guard Marina Mabrey and Williams took part in a brief 3-point shooting contest.
Saturday’s game will pit Bueckers’ Team Coop, coached by Aces coach Becky Hammon, against Clark and Wilson’s Team Spoon, led by Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve. The teams are playing for a combined $100,000 prize benefiting two Chicago youth sports organizations.

sources.news_title: Obama drops in at WNBA event inspiring ninth-grade girls at presidential center
sources.text:
Fourteen-year-old London Harris has dreams of someday being president of the United States, and on Friday morning she got to see a former commander in chief up close.
Former President Barack Obama surprised London, along with nearly 100 other ninth grade girls, during the third annual WNBA Changemaker Day at the recently opened Obama Presidential Center.
“It felt very surreal,” said London, a student at Dyett High School in Washington Park. “I was genuinely happy to see him and to listen to what he had to say.”
Obama popped into the center’s Elie Wiesel Auditorium just as a panel of speakers was discussing the power of perseverance.
“I know you’re all learning the power of perseverance, the power of resilience, the power of dreaming big,” WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert told the crowd. “And this person … has inspired hundreds of millions of people around the world and here in the United States.”
Obama then walked on stage to thunderous applause.
“Hello, everybody!” Obama exclaimed, wearing jeans and a white button-down shirt.
“Settle down now,” he said, smiling, as the crowd screamed.
“I wasn’t gonna let a bunch of amazing young athletes, scholars, hoopers come through my spot without saying hello,” he said. “I’m not gonna start shaking hands yet because mayhem will break loose.”
He began by telling the girls how proud he was of them and then spoke of his own experiences of being a dad to two daughters.
“Malia is now 28, Sasha is 25, but I remember like it was yesterday when they were your age,” Obama said. “We live in a world that is a lot more complicated for you guys than it was in some ways when I was coming up. There’s so much pressure and noise, and sometimes I think — especially for girls and young women — there’s social attitudes that tell you that you need to be one kind of way.”
He then encouraged the girls that they were on the right track.
“You are going to do wonderful things, and you need to have the confidence and power that’s inside you and your capacity to, you know, live out your dreams. … You’re gonna have to work hard, and it’s not going to be easy, but I’m confident it’s gonna happen.”
Obama joked with the girls about boys being “knuckleheads” and urged them to seek guidance from others.
“One of the most important things you can do as a young person is find people who are willing to help you,” Obama said.
“Find mentors. Find people who are doing the kinds of things you want to do and learn from them,” he added. “We only see the little fishbowl that we live in, but you know, it turns out there’s a whole big world out there full of possibilities. … The more you see out there that’s possible, the better off you’re going to be.”
Obama then joked about talking too long because he spots one of the girls “about to fall asleep.”
“I’m used to it. That’s what it’s like at the Obama dinner table,” he said.
Obama shook hands with some of the girls as they screamed, then took a selfie with the crowd before leaving the stage.
Aliyah Myles, a student at Chicago Vocational Career Academy, grew up with Obama being a constant presence in her household. She described the former president as a huge influential figure for her mother.
Next time Aliyah talks to her mother, she’ll get to tell her she shook Obama’s hand.
“I was freaking out, I was turnt, I almost passed out,” Aliyah, 14, said. “I was everywhere.”
The event kicked off just before 10 a.m. with comments from WNBA brand strategist Nina Kossoff. Friday’s gathering was among many events in Chicago this week tied to the WNBA All-Star Game, which will be held Saturday at the United Center.
“We’re powerful on our own, but when we come together, we can really make change,” Kossoff told the girls.
They also heard from a panel featuring Ari Chambers, an ESPN Journalist and commentator; Kizmet Mills, chief diversity officer at Nike; Linnae Harper, a former Chicago Sky player and now manager of athletics and sports leadership for the Obama Foundation; and Colie Edison, the WNBA’s chief growth officer.
It was the third WNBA Changemaker Day, and this year’s theme was “Finding My Superpower” — something each panelist touched on.
“When I think about the word ‘superpower,’ the first thing that comes to mind is doing the impossible,” Harper said. “My personal superpower is connecting people with their resources, providing a pathway for them to reach their goals.”
Others on the panel spoke on helping others through basketball, leadership and community efforts. The panelists then dived into explaining how they bounced back from their setbacks.
The students had begun trickling into the auditorium around 9:30 a.m. Some of the girls conversed and laughed while they waited, while others danced in their seats to Justin Timberlake’s “Can’t Stop the Feeling.”
In addition to Obama’s surprise appearance, students were inspired by the panelists to continue pursuing their dreams and rise through any adversity they face.
“This really inspired me to keep going, push everything, take time, be patient and just focus on my dreams and career,” said RaKaila Jefferson, 14.
For Aliyah, the event reinforced her aspirations to want to make an impact wherever she can.
“My goal is to make a change,” Aliyah said. “I want to be known somewhere around the world.”

sources.news_title: Obama Center subcontractor shuts down amid $4M fight, lays off 25
sources.text:
Weeks after the Obama Presidential Center’s star-studded opening in Chicago, a subcontractor who previously claimed his company was stiffed for nearly $4 million has shut down operations and laid off 25 union workers.
Mike Owen, the owner of Chicago-based Adamson Plumbing Contractors, told Fox News Digital that the financial fallout forced the company to abandon about half a dozen other construction jobs and left it on the verge of collapse. Owen described the shutdown as a painful decision he believed was necessary to save the company from bankruptcy.
“Laying off close to 30 people is something that no owner in our industry wants to do,” Owen said. “It’s a hard thing to do, especially when you know you can finish them and the company can still make money. But we were put in a pretty bad corner.”
Adamson, which performed its work on the center under the name Marsh-Adamson, has since filed a $1.72 million mechanic’s lien against the property, escalating the payment dispute into a legal fight.
The company is one of several subcontractors to report financial trouble after working on the center, which was promoted as a transformative economic opportunity for small and minority-owned businesses.
A previous Fox News Digital investigation identified several subcontractors — including Black-owned firms the project was specifically intended to support — that said they were owed money or had absorbed losses ranging from hundreds of thousands of dollars to millions. The largest dispute involves the Concrete Collective, which is seeking more than $40 million in additional payment.
Before the center opened, Owen said the project had left his company with $3.9 million in losses tied to delays, rework, labor overruns and changing project demands. He said he spent months negotiating with Lakeside Alliance, the project’s construction manager, before going public after failing to reach a resolution.
Against the backdrop of that larger dispute, Owen said the breaking point came around the time of the Obama Presidential Center’s opening celebration.
Owen said Adamson and Lakeside Alliance reached an agreement under which Adamson would provide two journeyman plumbers to perform last-minute “housekeeping” work on campus at premium nighttime rates.
In return, Owen said, Adamson was supposed to receive part of its outstanding payment days before the center opened on June 19. An email reviewed by Fox News Digital shows a Lakeside representative telling Owen that $100,000 would be released through Adamson’s May payment application.
Adamson completed the requested work, but the payment did not arrive on time, according to Owen, who said it was the company’s breaking point and left him with no choice but to suspend operations on June 25.
“We negotiated it in good faith,” he said. “Against my better judgment, I agreed [to do the work].”
“Not getting that large sum of money just kind of pulled the brakes on the train. It was just the final death blow to the company,” he added. “Rather than try to stretch it out and go bankrupt, I just decided the responsible thing was to shut it down. We’ll regroup, and we’ll see where we’re at come September.”
Owen said that the promised $100,000 retainage payment and around $35,000 for change orders payments have since arrived from Lakeside Alliance — more than two weeks after he suspended operations and laid off 25 workers.
Owen said the money helped reduce the company’s debt to one supplier but did not reverse the shutdown.
“It’s almost like too little, too late,” Owen said. “It probably would have just prolonged the inevitable at this point,” he said. “We’re still deep in the hole of what they owe us.”
Owen said Adamson has now moved out of its building and that he is working from home while turning the dispute over to his attorneys and determining whether the company has a future.
OBAMA CENTER ISN’T A TRADITIONAL PRESIDENTIAL LIBRARY. CRITICS SAY IT’S AN ACTIVISM CENTER.
Owen has escalated his nearly $4 million payment fight.
Documents reviewed by Fox News Digital show that Marsh-Adamson filed a $1.72 million mechanic’s lien against the Obama Presidential Center property, alleging it remains owed money for plumbing work performed on campus. A mechanic’s lien is a legal claim filed against a property by a contractor or supplier alleging that it has not been fully paid for completed work.
The lien is considerably lower than the approximately $3.9 million Owen says Adamson lost over the course of the project. Owen said the lien covers the amounts he believes are most readily documented, including unpaid fees, logged change orders and labor overruns supported by company records.
“It doesn’t mean that I’m not going to pursue the $3.9 million in change that we lost overall,” Owen said. “I’m still working with my legal team on that $3.9 million figure because I feel that it’s only right that we still hold ownership at the presidential center accountable.”
Owen said he had initially avoided filing a lawsuit or lien while attempting to negotiate a resolution.
“I’m not a litigious person, but at the same time, our legal system is there to protect the small guy,” Owen said. “I’m just going to have to fight this out legally from here on out, and these aren’t cheap costs.”
Last week’s payment will be deducted from the $1.72 million, he said.
Lakeside Alliance, a joint venture led by Turner Construction and four Black-owned Chicago construction firms, served as the project’s construction manager. The other firms are UJAMAA Construction, Powers & Sons Construction, Brown & Momen and Safeway Construction.
In a previous statement, Lakeside said approximately 475 contractors worked on the center. In its latest response, the alliance pointed to the project’s scale and said “contractual closeout continues long after the doors have opened” on major projects of such complexity.
“Lakeside Alliance remains committed to working through all outstanding matters to successfully close out the project,” a spokesperson said. Lakeside Alliance did not directly address Owen’s allegations, the layoffs or the $1.72 million lien.
WATCH: Subcontractor says his company is owed nearly $4M for work on Obama Center project
The Obama Foundation, former President Barack Obama’s private nonprofit organization that oversees the construction, said Lakeside was responsible for managing and paying subcontractors and that the foundation had no outstanding disputed charges with the alliance.
While it did not directly address Adamson’s allegations, the foundation said its financial support for firms working on the project exceeded industry standards.
“Our commitment began with a 15-day payment cycle, which is largely unheard of in major construction projects,” the foundation said in a statement, adding that it sometimes accelerated payment timelines or advanced payments months before work was completed.
The center has also faced scrutiny over its soaring price tag and promised taxpayer protections. Construction costs, initially projected at approximately $350 million, had climbed to $830 million by 2021 and have since reportedly surpassed $1 billion.
Meanwhile, just $1 million has been deposited into a promised $470 million reserve intended to protect Chicago taxpayers if the center encounters financial trouble.
Those questions have drawn added scrutiny because the Obama Foundation secured the 19.3-acre Jackson Park site through a 99-year lease requiring a one-time $10 payment.
Owen said the ordeal has left him financially and emotionally drained and uncertain whether he will ever restart Adamson Plumbing.
“This entire process really drained me out financially and emotionally,” Owen said. “So that’s where I’m at — just kind of in a holding pattern.”
Owen said the opening ceremony — which featured performances by Bruce Springsteen, Christina Aguilera, John Legend and U2’s Bono and The Edge, among others — only sharpened his anger. Against that celebratory backdrop, he said, the struggles of the workers who built the center went largely unrecognized.
Owen argued that Chicago’s proud protest culture had been conspicuously absent — and that the reaction would have been markedly different if the project were associated with figures such as Elon Musk or Ken Griffin, the Chicago billionaire whose name adorns the neighboring Griffin Museum of Science and Industry.
“There would be holy hell to pay,” Owen said. “They would be picketing. They would be storming the castle.”
Owen also singled out Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker, questioning why the pro-union governor had not addressed the layoffs or payment disputes.
“But he hasn’t said anything publicly about the union companies at the presidential center getting stiffed,” Owen said. “And it bothers me.”
Pritzker’s office did not respond to a request for comment.
Owen said he was not accusing former President Barack Obama of personal responsibility but believes the foundation should publicly acknowledge the subcontractors’ complaints and help seek a resolution.
“It’s become perfectly obvious to me that the ownership group there — they truthfully just don’t care,” he said. “I don’t know any other way to say it.”
Owen said contractors had held out hope that their disputes would be resolved once construction ended.
“But I think a lot of us out there, the main subcontractors, all still had this feeling that it was going to be worked out in the end — until it wasn’t,” he said.
Now, with Adamson’s future uncertain, Owen said the project has left him facing a personal turn he never saw coming.
“I mean, the only leverage I have now is just to continue speaking out and see where it goes,” he said. “But my career — it’s funny — I’m going to have to go find a job, which is fine. It’s just that I did not anticipate the completion of this project would take this turn.”
